title: Accurate Measurement and Documentation

unit.title: Clinical Office Practice and Patient Safety

sections.learningObjectives:
- Measure vital signs accurately using correct technique and equipment.
- Document measurements legibly, promptly, and with the correct units.
- Avoid transcription and documentation errors that could affect patient care.
- Recognize when a measurement is abnormal or uncertain and escalate appropriately within the assistant's scope.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Blood pressure has two numbers. If both numbers are below the 'safe lines' of 120 over 80, we call it normal — like a speed that is safely under the limit.

### Question 2

Think of the top number as the 'squeeze' when the heart pushes, and the bottom number as the 'rest' when the heart relaxes.

### Question 3

Elevated is like a yellow light — not yet high blood pressure, but a warning to keep an eye on it.

### Question 4

Stage 1 is like stepping onto the first step of a staircase — blood pressure has started to climb.

### Question 5

Stage 2 is when the numbers are clearly too high, like a speed well over the limit, and needs attention.

### Question 6

When a number is that high, it is like a smoke alarm going off — you tell a grown-up in charge right away instead of hiding it.

### Question 7

It is like letting a cup of cocoa sit a moment so it is just right — the body needs to settle before you measure.

### Question 8

Caffeine, smoking, and exercise rev the body up like a race car, so we let it idle first before reading the dial.

### Question 9

A full bladder is like a little balloon pressing inside, which can nudge the blood pressure up — so we empty it first.

### Question 10

A too-tight sleeve squeezes the arm too hard and makes the number read higher than it really is.

### Question 11

The cuff should sit at the same height as the heart, like keeping a measuring cup level so it reads correctly.

### Question 12

Talking makes the body work a little harder, like running while trying to be still — so we stay quiet and still.

### Question 13

Blood pressure uses its own special ruler called 'millimeters of mercury,' written as mm Hg.

### Question 14

If a number looks surprising, measure it again the right way before you believe it — like double-checking a scale.

### Question 15

Writing down which arm and how the patient was sitting is like labeling a photo with where and how it was taken.

### Question 16

Letting the air out slowly is like letting a balloon down gently so you can hear every little change.

### Question 17

The stethoscope listens at the soft spot inside the elbow, where the arm's main 'hose' runs close to the skin.

### Question 18

The cuff goes on the upper arm, just above the elbow crease, like putting a bracelet right above the bend.

### Question 19

A healthy body usually sits around 98.6°F, like a thermostat set to a comfortable room temperature.

### Question 20

The underarm is cooler than the mouth, so its temperature reads a little lower.

### Question 21

Writing '98.6' without saying mouth, ear, or underarm is like giving a distance without saying miles or kilometers.

### Question 22

A hot drink warms the mouth like a mug warms your hands — we wait a few minutes so the reading is the body's real temperature.

### Question 23

The cover is like a fresh glove for the thermometer, so one person's germs do not hop to the next person.

### Question 24

38 on the Celsius scale is hot, but 38 on the Fahrenheit scale is freezing — the scale label is what makes the number make sense.

### Question 25

A resting heart usually beats about once a second — that is the 60 to 100 range.

### Question 26

When a heartbeat skips around, we count the whole minute carefully so we do not miss any beats, then tell the person in charge.

### Question 27

We write down how many beats, whether they come in a steady rhythm, and how strong they feel.

### Question 28

The wrist is the easy, everyday spot to feel the heart's beat.

### Question 29

Your thumb has its own little heartbeat, so using it is like listening to two drums at once — we use the other fingers instead.

### Question 30

We count how many beats happen in one minute and label it 'beats per minute.'

### Question 31

A resting adult usually breathes in and out about every 3 to 5 seconds, which adds up to 12 to 20 a minute.

### Question 32

If someone knows you are counting their breaths, they might breathe differently — so we count quietly without them noticing.

### Question 33

To count breaths right, we watch the whole minute, like counting all the cars on a road instead of guessing.

### Question 34

We note not just how many breaths, but whether they are deep or shallow, even or uneven, and easy or hard.

### Question 35

We count breaths, so the label is 'breaths per minute.'

### Question 36

A healthy body keeps its oxygen level almost all the way full, like a gas tank near the top.

### Question 37

A cold finger, dark nail polish, or wiggling can trick the sensor, like a smudged camera lens making a blurry picture.

### Question 38

88% is like a gas gauge in the warning zone — you tell the person in charge instead of pretending it is full.

### Question 39

Oxygen level is shown as 'how full,' so we use a percent sign, like a battery percent.

### Question 40

To compare weights fairly, we weigh the person the same way every time, like weighing flour with the bowl always set to zero.

### Question 41

We weigh people in pounds or kilograms, and we write which one we used.

### Question 42

Standing tall like a ruler against the wall, with shoes off and head level, gives the truest height.

### Question 43

We measure how tall someone is in inches or centimeters and label which one.

### Question 44

To turn pounds into kilograms, we divide by 2.2 — 154 split into 2.2 pieces is about 70.

### Question 45

Mixing up digits is like writing a phone number with two numbers swapped — it needs to be fixed so the real number is recorded.

### Question 46

The pain scale is like a volume dial from 0 (silent, no pain) to 10 (turned all the way up).

### Question 47

Only the patient knows how much it hurts, so we write down their number, not our guess.

### Question 48

Pain is an important clue about how a patient is doing, so we record it right along with temperature and pulse.

### Question 49

Write clearly in pen and never scribble out or paint over mistakes, so the record stays honest and readable.

### Question 50

Fix a mistake by drawing one neat line through it and writing the correct word next to it, then signing and dating — like editing a paper in ink, not erasing history.

### Question 51

Write it down right away, like jotting a grocery list while you still remember the items.

### Question 52

A number without a unit is like a price without a dollar sign — add the label so everyone knows what it means.

### Question 53

When copying numbers, look back at the original and check your work, like double-checking a copied answer.

### Question 54

You cannot write down a score before the game is played — the number must come from a real measurement.

### Question 55

The person who takes the measurement writes it down, so the note is truthful and we know who did it.

### Question 56

If you forgot to write it, add it later with an honest note saying when it was really taken — never hide it or put it in the wrong chart.

### Question 57

Use only the official shorthand everyone agrees on, like using standard road signs instead of making up your own.

### Question 58

Write down exactly what you counted, like recording a test score exactly instead of rounding it to look nicer.

### Question 59

Every note needs a date and time stamp, like a timestamp on a photo, so we know exactly when it happened.

### Question 60

Record what the scale actually shows, and also write down what the patient says their home scale showed — keep the two separate.

### Question 61

A missing or extra zero is like a decimal point sliding over — it can turn 5 into 50, so we write numbers carefully.

### Question 62

If a number looks surprising, measure again to make sure it is real before you write it down and tell anyone.

### Question 63

If we cannot get a number, we say so honestly and tell the person in charge, instead of making one up.

### Question 64

Copy each number carefully from the paper, checking as you go, like copying a recipe without missing an ingredient.

### Question 65

Sign your name on your work so everyone knows who wrote it, like signing a letter.

### Question 66

Wash or sanitize your hands before and after each patient, like a chef cleaning hands between dishes.

### Question 67

Wipe down shared tools between patients, like cleaning a shared desk between users.

### Question 68

A probe cover is like a one-time wrapper — use it once, then throw it away for a fresh one.

### Question 69

Wipe the sensor clean before the next person uses it, like cleaning shared headphones.

### Question 70

Things meant for one use go in the trash after that one use, not back on the counter.

### Question 71

If someone just ran in, let them catch their breath and settle before you take the number.

### Question 72

One high number is not the whole story — measure again the right way before worrying or acting.

### Question 73

Use the right-sized band for the arm, like choosing the right belt size instead of forcing a small one.

### Question 74

A hot drink warms the mouth, so we wait a little while before reading the body's true temperature.

### Question 75

If the heartbeat is skipping, count the whole minute carefully and tell the person in charge.

### Question 76

If the breathing count looks high, count again carefully and tell the person in charge if it stays high.

### Question 77

If the sensor looks wobbly or the finger is cold, fix the setup and try again before believing the number.

### Question 78

If the weight jumps a lot, check the scale and weigh again before writing it down — like re-taring a kitchen scale.

### Question 79

Only the patient knows how much it hurts, so we write the number they tell us, even if they are smiling.

### Question 80

Record both numbers and label which arm each came from, then tell the person in charge about the difference.

### Question 81

Check the name and birthday twice, like making sure you are handing the right homework to the right person.

### Question 82

75 kilograms and 75 pounds are very different — ask which unit it is before writing it down.

### Question 83

Some numbers need a second look, and some need a call to the person in charge right away — the rules tell us which is which.

### Question 84

Vital signs are the body's basic checkup numbers: temperature, pulse, breathing, and blood pressure, plus often oxygen level.

### Question 85

Even on a busy day, write each patient's numbers down right away so nothing gets mixed up.
